title: USDA Certified Organic: Understanding the Basics | Agricultural Marketing Service
summary: USDA consumer page saying organic is protected by law, inspected yearly, traced from farm to store and shaped by public input.

assertions.quote: Specially trained organic inspectors visit organic farms and business yearly to confirm they still meet the organic standards.
Every organic operation is also subject to additional, unannounced inspections and testing.

verdicts.note: Certifiers must do unannounced inspections on at least 5 percent of operations and residue-test at least 5 percent each year.

7 CFR 205.670(c)-(d) requires certifiers to do periodic residue testing and to sample at least 5 percent of their operations each year (for-cause testing may also be required); the unannounced-inspection part comes from the SOE rule.
The SOE final rule requires certifiers to make unannounced inspections of at least 5 percent of the operations they certify, along with mass-balance audits at annual on-site inspections.

assertions.quote: trace organic products from the store all the way back to the farm

verdicts.note: The 2024 Strengthening Organic Enforcement rule added import certificates and supply-chain audits, but how much fraud it prevents is not yet measured.

SOE requires supply-chain traceability audits, labeled and traceable nonretail containers, and inspector checks back to the previous certified operation, which is a step-by-step trace toward the farm; the effect on fraud is asserted, not measured.

assertions.quote: These systems and processes confirm that what consumers buy is truly organic.
